articles.title: Rochdale man refused permission to appeal Manchester Airport assault sentence
articles.excerpt: Mohammed Fahir Amaaz, from Rochdale, has been refused permission to appeal against his 42-month sentence following assaults at Manchester Airport, according to sources.
articles.content_html:
A Rochdale man jailed after assaulting two police officers and a member of the public at Manchester Airport has been refused permission to appeal against his sentence, according to sources.

Mohammed Fahir Amaaz, 21, was sentenced at Liverpool Crown Court on 26 June 2026 to 42 months in prison. The Crown Prosecution Service confirmed his convictions were for assault occasioning actual bodily harm, assault by beating and assault on an emergency worker.

His renewed application for permission to appeal against sentence was scheduled before the Court of Appeal in London on Friday 16 October. The published court listing placed the case in Court 6 at 10am, under reference 202602577.

Before the hearing, his solicitors, Imran Khan and Partners, said a single judge had refused his initial application on 14 August. His legal team then renewed the application to the full court. Friday’s proceedings concerned permission to challenge his sentence.

The convictions arose from events at Manchester Airport on 23 July 2024. According to the CPS, the incident began when Amaaz assaulted a passenger inside the Terminal 2 Starbucks and continued in another part of the airport when police arrived to arrest him. One officer suffered a broken nose.

The offences for which he was sentenced involved member of the public Abdulkareem Hamzah Abbas Ismaeil, PC Lydia Ward and PC Ellie Cook.

A separate allegation involving PC Zachary Marsden must be distinguished from those convictions. Amaaz and his brother, Muhammad Amaad, also from Rochdale, faced that allegation, but two juries were unable to reach verdicts. In May 2026, the prosecution offered no further evidence and not guilty verdicts were recorded.

The sentence application listed on Friday was in Mohammed Fahir Amaaz’s name. Rochdale Daily will update this report if the court’s detailed reasons or a further statement from his legal representatives become available.

articles.title: St Cuthbert’s RC High School Closes Following Bomb Threat
articles.excerpt: St Cuthbert’s RC High School in Rochdale was evacuated and closed on 16 October after receiving a suspected bomb threat. All students and staff were reported safe, and police are investigating the incident.
articles.content_html:
St Cuthbert’s RC High School in Rochdale was evacuated and closed on Friday morning, 16 October, after staff received a communication regarding a possible bomb threat. The school, located on Shaw Road, implemented emergency procedures to ensure the safety of all students and staff.

In response to the threat, Greater Manchester Police were called to the scene, and the school entered a lockdown as a precautionary measure. A spokesperson for the school confirmed that all children and staff were safe and accounted for during the incident. The police assessed the situation and indicated that the call was likely a hoax.

The St Teresa of Calcutta Catholic Academy Trust, which oversees the school, stated that specialist security operatives would conduct a thorough sweep of the premises to determine if any further action was necessary. Parents and carers were informed that they could collect their children or give permission for them to travel home safely.

The school is expected to reopen as normal on Monday, 19 October, pending the outcome of the police investigation. Authorities have urged the public to refrain from speculation on social media regarding false rumours related to the incident.

articles.title: East Middleton councillor questions parking charge warning after petrol station breakdown
articles.excerpt: Labour councillor Georgina Jacques says she was warned about a parking charge while waiting for the RAC after her car broke down on Oldham Road.
articles.content_html:
Labour councillor Georgina Jacques says she was warned she could face a parking charge while waiting for recovery after her car broke down at a petrol station on Oldham Road.

Councillor Jacques, who represents East Middleton on Rochdale Borough Council, described the incident in a public Facebook post, asking whether the business could charge her when her vehicle would not start.

Writing about the breakdown, she said:

“So I’ve broken down in Petrol station on Oldham Road.

“Yes another car that’s absolutely useless ”

She then described a conversation with a member of staff:

“Anyway the guy working there said, I am gunna get charged for parking when his boss comes, as hes saying I can’t stay waiting for RAC!!! I can’t move my car obviously as it won’t start ”

According to her account, the vehicle was beside the station’s tyre inflation equipment. She wrote:

“it’s at the tyre pumper upper so not really blocking anywhere.

“So is this legal does anyone know surly they can’t charge me for breaking down.”

Councillor Jacques said the RAC had given her an estimated arrival window between 9.30pm and 11.30pm.

The screenshot does not establish that a parking charge was subsequently issued, how much was allegedly proposed, or which parking conditions applied. The petrol station is not named in the post, and its account of the conversation is not available.

Could she actually be charged?

A private parking operator can issue a parking charge where it alleges that a driver breached the site’s parking conditions. That is a civil payment demand, rather than a criminal charge. Whether a demand would be enforceable in this particular case cannot be determined from the Facebook post alone. The signage, terms, circumstances of the breakdown and evidence of the recovery arrangements would matter.

However, a breakdown gives a motorist a strong reason to challenge a ticket issued while waiting for repairs or recovery. Citizens Advice specifically identifies being unable to move a broken-down vehicle as grounds for an appeal. That does not guarantee automatic cancellation, but it means a demand should not simply be assumed valid.

Independent parking appeals service POPLA also identifies evidence of a breakdown and a recovery callout as relevant when exceptional circumstances prevented a driver from complying with parking conditions.

Drivers in this situation should retain recovery booking messages, attendance records and photographs of the parking signs. The Competition and Markets Authority advises motorists to preserve evidence when a breakdown occurs and to challenge a disputed charge rather than ignore it.

For now, Councillor Jacques’s post establishes that she reported being warned about a possible charge. It does not establish that she received one or that any payment was legally owed.

We hope Councillor Jacques is rescued promptly and back to her council duties in the morning—with her car feeling rather more cooperative.

articles.title: Teenager Jailed for Fatal Crash in Middleton After Teaching Himself to Drive
articles.excerpt: An 18-year-old has been sentenced to nearly seven years in prison after causing the death of a grandfather in Middleton while driving unlicensed and recklessly.
articles.content_html:
A teenager has been sentenced to nearly seven years in prison for causing the death of a grandfather in Middleton while driving unlicensed and recklessly. Ruhul Islam, now 18, taught himself to drive by watching YouTube videos and was behind the wheel of his brother's Nissan Micra when he struck Terence James, 78, on Shawbury Street on September 29, 2024.

During a hearing at Manchester Crown Court on October 13, it was revealed that Islam had borrowed the car to make takeaway deliveries for a local business. Witnesses reported seeing him swerving through traffic, running red lights, and driving aggressively shortly before the crash. Mr James was crossing the road with his 10-year-old granddaughter when he was hit, suffering severe injuries that led to his death the following day after life support was withdrawn.

Judge Kate Cornell described the vehicle as a 'dangerous weapon' in the hands of someone unqualified to drive. She stated that Mr James would likely still be alive had Islam adhered to traffic laws. The court heard that Islam initially attempted to conceal his involvement in the crash, claiming his older brother was driving at the time.

The incident has raised concerns about road safety and the consequences of unlicensed driving. Following the sentencing, it is expected that discussions around stricter enforcement of driving regulations may take place, although no specific measures have been announced yet.

evidence_sources.captured_text: Unlicensed teen taught himself to drive on YouTube, ran red lights, then killed beloved dad in Middleton horror crash - Manchester Evening News ‌ ‌ Skip to main content Manchester Evening News: Number one for news, opinion, sport & celebrity news Unlicensed teen taught himself to drive on YouTube, ran red lights, then killed beloved dad in Middleton horror crash Ruhul Islam was sentenced to six years and 11 months in prison following the death of Terence James View 4 Images Ruhul Islam had manipulated his brother into allowing him to use his car when Terence James was killed Add to preferred sources News Bethan Finighan Science and Innovation Writer 17:13, 14 Oct 2026 Updated 22:36, 14 Oct 2026 An unlicensed teenager who taught himself to drive by watching YouTube videos swerved through traffic and ran red lights before ploughing his older brother's Nissan Micra into a granddad who was crossing the road with his 10-year-old granddaughter. Terence James , 78, died after being struck by the vehicle on Shawbury Street, Middleton , on September 29, 2024. Yesterday (October 13), Manchester Crown Court heard how Ruhul Islam had borrowed the car to make takeaway deliveries at the time of the offence. The 16-year-old was seen overtaking and undertaking vehicles, running red lights and weaving between lanes in the moments before the crash. Click here to hear the latest from Manchester's courts in our newsletter ‌ Now 18, he has been jailed for nearly seven years. Passing sentence, Judge Kate Cornell said: "The vehicle essentially became a dangerous weapon in the hands of someone unable to use it." View 4 Images Terence Lewis James, 78, who died after being struck by a car in Middleton (Image: Family submit) She said Mr James would still be alive had Islam driven on the correct side of the road, telling him: "That momentary lapse of judgement caused the tragedy that everyone in this room has to deal with for the rest of their lives… None of them will ever be the same again." The court heard Islam initially tried to hide that he had been driving and instead said his older brother was behind the wheel. Investigators later found Islam and his 16-year-old friend had been making deliveries for Chilli Pot takeaway in Middleton - a business owned by family friends - at the time of the offence. ‌ Shortly after 7pm, Islam turned right from Grimshaw Lane into Shawbury Street in Middleton and struck Mr James as he crossed the road. He was on the right carriageway of the road when he was hit, having already crossed the left carriageway. Prosecuting, Philip Hall told the court Islam "cut the corner by a significant margin". Mr James suffered a serious head injury and was rushed to Salford Royal hospital, where his condition deteriorated and he never regained consciousness. His family made the heartbreaking decision to withdraw life support the following evening. A witness who was in a nearby car park on Shawbury Street heard the collision and saw Mr James lying in the road. She gave him first aid and said she was 'surprised the two Asian males were not helping', prosecutors told the court. ‌ Another witness, the court heard, saw two men get out of the Nissan Micra before running away from the car. He said one man later emerged from the nearby takeaway and repeatedly insisted his brother had been driving and was only travelling at 10mph. The court was shown dashcam footage from the vehicle in the hour before the collision, which showed the car swerving between lanes in wet weather , "aggressive" overtaking and undertaking and driving through red lights. View 4 Images Ruhul Islam has been jailed for nearly seven years (Image: Greater Manchester Police) Four minutes before striking Mr James, footage showed Islam overtaking a vehicle into the opposing lane, before undertaking into a cycle lane. Two minutes before the collision, the vehicle made another "completely unnecessary" manoeuvre by contravening a traffic island on the other side of the road, the court heard. ‌ Islam initially failed to come forward as the driver after the fatal collision, with his older brother putting himself forward instead. After an investigation established Islam had been behind the wheel, both brothers were arrested at their home in Chadderton on November 24, 2024. In part of a police interview read to the court, Islam admitted teaching himself to drive by watching videos on YouTube and manipulating his brother, who has autism, to get the keys to his car. In her final remarks, Judge Cornell said: "You now accept that you manipulated and misled him to get his keys. You told him not to tell anyone." ‌ Judge Cornell also questioned how the adults in Islam's life "turned a blind eye" to his driving without a license, given he was just 16 years old and working for a family friend's business. View 4 Images Terence James, 78 (Image: Family submit) Defending, Michael Avery said Islam had no previous convictions or cautions and had received 11 positive character references, including one from Oldham Council Labour councillor Mohon Ali. He said the offence has had a "genuine impact on him and those closest to him", leaving Islam "withdrawn" and "spending more time in his room". The defence also referred to the impact of the offence on his mental health. ‌ Judge Cornell later said she accepted Islam's remorse was genuine and that he had experienced flashbacks and nightmares following the collision. In emotional statements read to the court, Mr James' grandson Harry James described him as a "soft and kind" man who was the "glue of the family". Caroline, one of Mr James's four children, described her father as the "kindest person I knew", saying he "would do anything for anyone and wouldn't hurt a fly". Describing the aftermath of the collision, Caroline rushed to the scene after her daughter, Daisy, returned to the house "hysterical", shouting that "grandad had been knocked down". ‌ She wrote in her statement that she saw her father on the ground as a woman put him in the recovery position. She said a man came out of the takeaway and apologised for what had happened. When she asked if he had been driving, she said he told her: "No, my brother, he's got autism". Addressing Islam, she wrote: "I have never been able to get over how the person in the dock lied to me. You didn't call an ambulance. You could see how upset I was and still came over and lied to my face…But you still tried to blame your brother." Islam pleaded guilty to causing death by dangerous driving after initially pleading not guilty. He also pleaded guilty to causing death while unlicensed and uninsured and perverting the course of justice. ‌ Sentencing, Judge Cornell said Mr James had been "suddenly and heartbreakingly taken from his family". She said Islam's driving had been "clearly unrestrained by the rules of the road that we all have to follow and of course you never properly learned". The judge said there had been an element of "excitement and showing off" in his driving, with footage showing him overtaking and undertaking vehicles, driving in hatched areas and cycle lanes, and twice going through red lights. "Had you driven on the correct side of the road you would not have caused his death and he would be alive today," Judge Cornell said, adding that it was "only good fortune" that Mr James's granddaughter was not also hit or injured. Ruhul Islam, of Little Cot Close, Chadderton, was sentenced to six years and 11 months. He has also been disqualified from driving for eight years after his release. articles.title: UK Lawmaker Threatens Visa Bans Over Rochdale Grooming Gang Ringleader
articles.excerpt: A UK lawmaker has warned Pakistan of potential flight and visa bans if it does not accept the return of a ringleader from the Rochdale grooming gang.
articles.content_html:
A UK lawmaker has threatened to impose flight and visa bans on Pakistan if the country does not accept the return of a ringleader from the Rochdale grooming gang. This warning highlights ongoing tensions regarding the handling of individuals involved in serious crimes abroad.

The comments come amid scrutiny of the UK government's approach to dealing with foreign nationals convicted of crimes in the UK. The ringleader, associated with a notorious grooming gang in Rochdale, has reportedly not been returned to Pakistan despite calls for his extradition.

This situation raises concerns about international relations and the management of criminal justice across borders. Local authorities in Rochdale have emphasised the need for effective measures to ensure accountability for those guilty of such crimes, regardless of nationality.

As developments unfold, it remains to be seen how the UK government will respond to Pakistan's stance on this matter.

articles.title: Bury Man Faces Trial for Alleged Aggravated Burglary in Rochdale
articles.excerpt: Loui Dyer, 32, from Bury, is accused of an aggravated burglary on Long Street, Rochdale, involving a knuckle duster. His trial is set for November 18 at Manchester Crown Court.
articles.content_html:
A 32-year-old man from Bury is set to face trial for an alleged aggravated burglary that took place in Rochdale. Loui Dyer, of Bradshaw House, Walmersley Road, is accused of entering a property on Long Street as a trespasser on April 24 and stealing £250.

Court records indicate that Dyer was allegedly in possession of a knuckle duster with a knife attachment during the incident. He has pleaded not guilty to the charges and is currently remanded in custody.

Dyer's trial is scheduled for November 18 at 10.30am at Manchester Crown Court, Crown Square. Two other individuals, Peter Wilson, 26, of Houghton Close, Rochdale, and Rose Murphy, 30, of Dale Street Mews, Heywood, are also implicated in the case. Both Wilson and Murphy have also pleaded not guilty and are remanded in custody.

The outcome of this trial could have implications for local residents, particularly regarding safety and crime in the area, as the case highlights ongoing concerns about burglary and violent crime.

articles.title: New Support Website Launched for Survivors of Child Sexual Abuse in Rochdale
articles.excerpt: A new website, IAmReady.org, offers tailored support for survivors of child sexual abuse and exploitation, providing resources to help them navigate investigations and review closed cases.
articles.content_html:
Survivors of child sexual abuse and exploitation in Rochdale can now access a new support service designed to help them understand their options regarding investigations into their allegations. The website, IAmReady.org, offers tailored advice and guidance based on individual needs, enabling victims to make informed decisions about their cases.

Developed in collaboration with survivors, the website provides trauma-informed information in an accessible format. Users can navigate the site at their own pace, with features that allow them to save their progress and exit quickly for privacy. The platform also includes options for users to request a review of their cases if they were previously closed by the Crown Prosecution Service or local police, particularly under the Victims’ Right to Review (VRR) or the Child Sexual Abuse Review Panel (CSARP).

This initiative is part of Operation Beaconport, which was established in November 2025 following Baroness Casey’s audit of group-based child sexual abuse and exploitation. The operation is currently reviewing hundreds of cases where no further action was taken between January 1, 2010, and March 31, 2025. Victims wishing to submit information about previously closed cases involving group-based offending will have their requests reviewed by specially trained officers from the operation.

The launch of IAmReady.org aims to empower survivors by providing them with the necessary tools and support to navigate their experiences and seek justice. For those affected, this resource may represent a significant step towards healing and accountability.

articles.title: Milnrow Woman's Appeal Against Animal Ban Rejected by Court
articles.excerpt: A Milnrow woman has had her appeal against a five-year ban on keeping animals dismissed by a judge after her dog was put down due to untreated injuries.
articles.content_html:
A woman from Milnrow has had her appeal against a five-year ban on keeping animals rejected by a judge at Manchester Crown Court. Anne Marie Wood was previously sentenced for causing unnecessary suffering to her dog, Tilly, who had to be euthanised after suffering from a broken leg that went untreated.

The RSPCA received a tip-off in December 2024 regarding Tilly's condition and found the Bichon Frise visibly lame and hesitant to put weight on her front leg. Wood initially refused to cooperate with inspectors but eventually allowed them into her home. She claimed the injury occurred when Tilly fell while being passed through a front window and stated that she could not afford the necessary veterinary treatment, which was estimated to be between £400 and £500.

Despite the RSPCA's offer to take Tilly to their Greater Manchester Animal Hospital for examination, Wood declined. When Tilly was eventually seen by a vet, it was determined that her injuries were severe and that treatment could not restore an acceptable quality of life. The decision was made to put her to sleep to prevent further suffering.

Wood, of St James Street, pleaded guilty at Tameside Magistrates Court on July 31 and received an 18-month prison sentence, suspended for one year, along with a ten-day Rehabilitation Activity Requirement and a nine-month drug rehabilitation programme. Following the rejection of her appeal on September 30, Wood remains banned from keeping animals for five years.

articles.title: Sara Rowbotham: the Rochdale health worker who raised 181 safeguarding alerts
articles.excerpt: Sara Rowbotham repeatedly raised concerns about vulnerable young people while working for Rochdale’s Crisis Intervention Team, later giving evidence to Parliament about the response to child sexual exploitation in the town.
articles.content_html:
Sara Rowbotham became one of the most recognisable figures associated with the response to child sexual exploitation in Rochdale after repeatedly raising concerns about vulnerable young people while working for the town’s NHS Crisis Intervention Team.

Rowbotham worked as the Crisis Intervention Team Co-ordinator and Sexual Health Improvement Specialist. The team was established in 2004 and supported thousands of young people, including those who disclosed concerns about sexual abuse and exploitation.

In evidence to the House of Commons Home Affairs Committee in November 2012, Rowbotham told MPs that, over a period covering the years from 2005 to 2011, her team had identified referrals involving 103 young people.

She also told the committee that she had made 181 alerts to Children’s Social Care about concerns involving young people.

Asked whether she believed police and social services had worked together effectively, Rowbotham said this had happened “very rarely” in the early period and that she had subsequently begun making the Safeguarding Children Unit aware of the referrals so that strategy meetings could be convened.

The committee also heard evidence from other senior officials about the handling of the information. The subsequent Home Affairs Committee report described missed opportunities and examined the response of children's social care and police to child sexual exploitation in Rochdale.

Rowbotham told MPs that she had repeatedly tried to make protective services aware of the vulnerability of young people and that she believed agencies had failed to provide a sufficiently comprehensive and coordinated response.

The evidence came after the prosecution of nine men in Rochdale in 2012 for serious sexual offences against girls. The case prompted wider scrutiny of how authorities had responded to reports of child sexual exploitation.

Rowbotham continued to speak publicly about the response. In 2014, she was made redundant from her role. Contemporary reporting by ITV News and The Guardian documented her concerns about the handling of the case and the impact of losing her position.

Her story later reached a much wider audience when the BBC drama Three Girls was broadcast in May 2017, with Maxine Peake portraying Rowbotham.

A petition calling for Rowbotham to be formally recognised attracted more than 100,000 signatures within days of the programme airing and ultimately exceeded 275,000 signatures, according to contemporary reports.

Rowbotham subsequently entered local politics. She was elected as a councillor for North Middleton in 2015 and went on to serve as Deputy Leader of Rochdale Borough Council and as a cabinet member.

Her public recognition also continued. She received a Special Recognition Award at the NHS Heroes Awards in 2018 and was made an honorary member of the NSPCC Council that year. In 2021, she was appointed MBE for services to young people.

Rowbotham’s evidence to Parliament remains part of the official record of the scrutiny that followed the Rochdale child sexual exploitation cases. Her account of the 181 alerts, and questions about how information held by frontline services was acted upon, formed part of the wider examination of safeguarding failures in the town.

Source: House of Commons Home Affairs Committee evidence and report; contemporary reporting by ITV News and The Guardian; Rochdale Borough Council records.

articles.content_html:
Latest, 08:30, Tuesday 1 September: six teenage boys have been arrested in connection with the stabbing of a 13-year-old boy in Rochdale town centre on Saturday night, 29 August. Two were arrested on Sunday and have since been released on bail. Four more were arrested on Monday and remain in custody. All six were held on suspicion of assault and possession of a bladed article, Greater Manchester Police said. The injured boy remains in hospital receiving treatment.

This is Rochdale Daily's single live story on the incident. It is updated in place, newest first, only when Greater Manchester Police or another primary source confirms a development. Earlier separate reports have been folded into this page; see the correction note at the foot.

What we know

The boy was stabbed during a serious assault in the town centre, near the Riverside shopping centre, on the evening of Saturday 29 August. Police described the incident as a serious assault alongside wider disorder in the town centre that night. He was taken to hospital, where he remains.

Monday 31 August: GMP confirmed four further arrests, all teenage boys, on suspicion of assault and possession of a bladed article. The two boys arrested on Sunday were released on bail while enquiries continue. Detective Superintendent Richard Hunt said the force was continuing to make progress on the investigation and that violence on the streets would not be tolerated.

Monday 31 August: the Section 60 order covering Rochdale town centre was extended until 3pm on Tuesday 1 September. Under Section 60 of the Criminal Justice and Public Order Act, officers can stop and search people in the designated area without needing reasonable suspicion.

Sunday 30 August: GMP announced two arrests and put a 24-hour Section 60 order in place for the town centre from 3pm. Chief Inspector Michael Barton, neighbourhoods lead for GMP's Rochdale district, said detectives were reviewing CCTV, gathering witness statements and analysing intelligence to identify everyone involved.

Saturday 29 August: a 13-year-old boy was stabbed in the town centre. GMP log 2750 of 29/08/2026.

What we do not know

Police have not released the boy's condition beyond confirming he remains in hospital, and have not said what led to the assault. No one has been charged. Rochdale Daily will not name anyone arrested and will not publish speculation about motive or identity while the investigation is live.

How to help the investigation

Anyone who witnessed the incident, was in Rochdale town centre on Saturday evening, or has mobile phone, CCTV or dashcam footage is asked to contact GMP on 101, quoting log 2750 of 29/08/2026, or via the LiveChat function at gmp.police.uk. Information can be given anonymously to Crimestoppers on 0800 555 111.

articles.title: Police promise increased patrols around The Strand after resident reports verbal abuse
articles.excerpt: Police say they will speak to two shops and increase patrols around The Strand and Kirkway after a resident reported being verbally abused by a man who had been begging in the area.
articles.content_html:
Police have told a Kirkholt resident that patrols will be increased around The Strand and Kirkway following a reported incident involving a man begging and verbally abusing her last week.

The resident said she received a positive telephone call from police on Monday afternoon after reporting the incident at The Strand.

According to the resident, officers said they intend to speak to staff at two shops in the area as part of efforts to identify the man involved. If he can be identified, police indicated that appropriate action would be considered.

The resident said officers also told her that police are taking this type of behaviour seriously and intend to increase patrols around The Strand and Kirkway.

The response will be welcomed by residents and businesses concerned about antisocial behaviour in the area. The Strand is an important neighbourhood hub used by families, shoppers and people accessing local community facilities, and residents should be able to use the area without feeling intimidated or being subjected to abuse.

Begging itself and antisocial or abusive behaviour are not necessarily the same thing, and people experiencing homelessness or financial hardship should not automatically be treated as offenders. However, threatening, intimidating or verbally abusive behaviour can be reported to police, particularly where somebody feels unsafe.

The reported incident remains an allegation and Rochdale Daily is not identifying the man involved. No suggestion is made that he has committed a criminal offence unless and until police establish the circumstances and take any appropriate action.

Anyone experiencing threatening or abusive behaviour can report it to Greater Manchester Police. Where there is an immediate danger or a crime is in progress, residents should call 999.

articles.title: Fraudsters who fought over the pensioners they were fleecing jailed - Rochdale woman among victims of £97,000 scam
articles.excerpt: Eight people have been sentenced over a roofing scam that took £97,000 from five elderly victims in three months - including £7,800 from a 77-year-old Rochdale woman. Two victims died before seeing justice.
articles.content_html:
A group of fraudsters who squabbled over the vulnerable pensioners they were ripping off have been jailed - including for a scam that stripped £7,800 from a 77-year-old Rochdale woman.

Eight people have now been sentenced over a ruthless building scam that took around £97,000 from five elderly victims across England in the space of just three months. They pleaded guilty to conspiracy to defraud and related money laundering offences.

The fraudsters pressured pensioners into handing over cash, making bank transfers and signing large cheques for roof repairs that were never carried out.

The 77-year-old woman from Rochdale was pressured into handing over cash, making transfers and signing cheques totalling £7,800, forced to dip into savings to pay for work that was never done.

Some of the most disturbing details emerged when police examined messages recovered from the offenders' phones. Two rival groups of scammers had independently targeted the same vulnerable man in Ellesmere Port. They regularly took him to local cash machines and made him withdraw money, and also used his bank card to buy themselves food and groceries. As his money ran out, the two rival factions clashed over who had the right to keep defrauding him.

The offending only came to light when the man's regular direct debits started to bounce because his account had been drained, and he turned to a friend for help.

Other victims included an elderly man in Ellesmere Port persuaded to write cheques worth £34,500 for roof work that was never completed, an elderly woman in Coventry whose signed blank cheques were written out for £13,000, and an elderly woman in Corby who had unnecessary roof repairs carried out to a poor standard.

The stolen money was laundered through the bank accounts of several accomplices before being spent on expensive meals and luxury Rolex watches.

Tragically, two of the elderly victims died before the gang finally appeared in court and never saw justice served.

Detective Constable Rob Mackay, of Ellesmere Port CID, who led the investigation, described it as a lengthy and complex inquiry.

The case is a reminder of how doorstep criminals operate: unsolicited callers claiming urgent roof or building problems, pressure to pay immediately in cash or by cheque, and escorted trips to the bank. Trading standards advice is never to agree to work from a cold caller, to seek quotes from traders you approach yourself, and to talk to a trusted friend or family member before parting with money. Anyone who believes an elderly relative or neighbour is being targeted can contact police on 101, or Action Fraud.

articles.title: 60 police officer misconduct cases in a single year. To protect and serve?
articles.excerpt: A Rochdale Daily analysis of Greater Manchester Police's own published misconduct reports found 60 officer misconduct case entries in 2025 - with 41 ending in dismissal or a finding that dismissal would have followed.
articles.content_html:
The words "To Protect & Serve" represent one of the most recognisable ideals of modern policing. The overwhelming majority of police officers go to work every day to protect the public with professionalism and integrity.

But Greater Manchester Police's own published misconduct records reveal another side of policing that deserves public scrutiny.

An analysis by Rochdale Daily of GMP's published quarterly misconduct outcome reports found 60 police officer misconduct case entries during 2025.

Those cases involved allegations ranging from criminal convictions and violence to discriminatory behaviour, misuse of confidential police systems and failures to investigate serious offences.

Among the allegations recorded by GMP were: assault occasioning actual bodily harm; drink-driving convictions; positive drug tests, including cocaine; sexual assault; domestic abuse and coercive control allegations considered through misconduct proceedings; criminal damage; misuse of police computer systems; racist, misogynistic, homophobic and discriminatory messages; sexual harassment of colleagues; inappropriate contact with vulnerable members of the public; failures to investigate allegations of rape; and breaches of police business interest regulations.

The outcomes were equally striking.

Of the 60 officer misconduct case entries reviewed, 19 resulted in dismissal without notice. A further 22 resulted in findings that the officer would have been dismissed had they still been serving with Greater Manchester Police. Six resulted in final written warnings, five in written warnings, and two allegations were not proven. The remaining cases resulted in other disciplinary outcomes, including practice improvement or findings below the threshold for gross misconduct.

In other words, 41 of the 60 cases resulted in either dismissal or a finding that dismissal would have been the outcome had the officer remained in service.

Every misconduct case has its own facts and circumstances, and misconduct proceedings are separate from criminal court proceedings. Some officers had already resigned or retired before their hearings concluded, which is why some outcomes are recorded as "would have been dismissed."

It is also important to recognise that Greater Manchester Police employs thousands of officers. The misconduct cases published during 2025 represent a small proportion of the overall workforce, and the published reports do not suggest that misconduct is typical of policing within the force.

Nevertheless, policing relies on public confidence. Every misconduct finding, particularly those involving violence, dishonesty, discrimination, abuse of authority or failures to investigate serious crime, has the potential to undermine that trust.

Transparency matters.

That is why Rochdale Daily has launched Police Watch, an ongoing series examining police accountability using official records, misconduct decisions, court judgments, Freedom of Information responses and reports from independent oversight bodies.

This investigation is not about attacking policing. It is about ensuring that the public can see how misconduct is identified, investigated and dealt with when officers fall below the standards expected of them.

Methodology: This analysis is based on Greater Manchester Police's published quarterly misconduct outcome reports covering January to December 2025. The figure of 60 refers to police officer misconduct case entries published by GMP. Police staff cases were excluded from the analysis. Because some published cases are anonymised, the reports do not always allow confirmation that every entry relates to a different individual, and therefore the figure should be understood as the number of recorded officer misconduct cases rather than confirmed unique officers.

Sources: Greater Manchester Police's official published misconduct outcome reports - GMP Misconduct Outcomes, January to March 2025; April to June 2025; July to September 2025; and October to December 2025.

articles.title: Elderly lady found after incredible community effort
articles.excerpt: A woman in her 70s who went missing in Newhey has been found after hundreds of residents joined Greater Manchester Police in an extraordinary community search.
articles.content_html:
An elderly woman who went missing in Newhey has been found following an extraordinary community effort involving hundreds of local residents.

Christine, who is in her 70s, was reported missing earlier in the evening, prompting an urgent response from Greater Manchester Police and a huge mobilisation across Newhey and the surrounding area.

As concern grew, residents left their homes to help officers search on the ground. People walked streets, paths and open spaces, checked nearby areas and shared information rapidly across community groups in an effort to bring Christine home.

The response was remarkable. Hundreds of people are understood to have assisted either directly with searches or by sharing appeals and helping coordinate information alongside GMP.

At around 11pm, local woman Charlotte Rigby found Christine. In a touching detail after hours of worry, Christine was found clutching a bunch of flowers.

News that she had been located was met with enormous relief across the community, bringing a frightening evening to the best possible conclusion.

Tonight demonstrated Newhey and the wider Rochdale borough at its very best. Residents did not simply share a post and hope for good news. They put on their shoes, went outside and actively helped search for someone who needed them.

Credit must also go to Greater Manchester Police and everyone who supported the search, but special recognition is due to the countless members of the public who gave their time and refused to give up.

The borough should be very proud tonight. This was community spirit in its purest form, and the outcome is the great news everyone had been hoping for.

Out of respect for Christine and her family, no further personal or medical details should be shared unless released through official channels.

articles.title: Shabir Ahmed barred from Rochdale under strict licence conditions as government pushes to deport him
articles.excerpt: The Rochdale grooming gang ringleader is excluded from the borough under his licence conditions, is living under 24-hour supervision at an undisclosed location outside the area, and faces active government efforts to deport him.
articles.content_html:
Shabir Ahmed, the ringleader of the Rochdale grooming gang jailed in 2012, was released from prison on licence on 2 July after serving 14 years of a 22-year sentence for multiple rape and sexual offences against young girls. Rochdale Daily can confirm, based on conditions set out by the Home Office and Ministry of Justice, that he is not living in Rochdale and is barred from entering the borough.

His licence conditions include an exclusion zone covering Rochdale and Oldham, electronic GPS tagging to monitor his movements, a requirement to live in approved accommodation staffed 24 hours a day, and a ban from his last known address in Oldham. The Ministry of Justice has said he is subject to the toughest supervision possible and would be returned to prison immediately if any condition were breached.

Ahmed, 73, was initially placed in approved premises in Accrington, Lancashire. After that address was shared on social media, prompting protests in the town and calls from the local MP for his removal, he was moved. The government has not confirmed his current location, and Rochdale Daily will not publish unverified claims about his whereabouts. Speculation of that kind has already forced one relocation and puts bystanders at the shared addresses at risk.

The question survivors and residents have pressed hardest is why he remains in the country at all. Ahmed was stripped of his British citizenship after his conviction, and victims had been led to believe he would be deported on release. It has since emerged that a provision of the Immigration Act 1971 prevents the removal of Commonwealth citizens who arrived in the United Kingdom before 1973, as Ahmed did as a teenager in 1967.

The government says it is exploring every option to remove him. Downing Street has confirmed talks with Pakistan, and a Home Office minister told the Commons that “all options are on the table”, saying the government would not give up its efforts given the nature of his crimes. Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood has set out plans to amend the 1971 Act so that people convicted of the most serious offences, including child sexual exploitation, can no longer rely on its protections, and ministers have indicated emergency legislation could be considered.

Pakistan, however, has publicly rejected the request. Officials in Islamabad have said responsibility for Ahmed lies with Britain, where he was brought up, and he is reported to have renounced his Pakistani citizenship, which complicates removal further even if the British law changes. The Prime Minister's spokesman has declined to comment on specific proposals while the talks continue.

The pressure on ministers is cross-party. The Conservatives have proposed amending the government's immigration legislation to close the loophole, with their leader urging ministers to adopt the change and the shadow home secretary suggesting visa sanctions or cuts to aid if Pakistan continues to refuse. Greater Manchester's mayor is among those who have called publicly for deportation, and the MP for Hyndburn, where Ahmed was first housed, has demanded he be barred from the North West entirely.

Campaigners including former Greater Manchester Police detective Maggie Oliver have criticised the handling of the release, saying victims learned of it through social media and continue to live with fear that the authorities have not taken seriously.

Rochdale Daily will update this article as official information is released. Readers should treat any claim about Ahmed's location that does not come from the Home Office, the Ministry of Justice, Greater Manchester Police or the courts as unverified.

articles.title: Editorial: Justice remains unfinished in Rochdale
articles.excerpt: More than a decade after the Rochdale grooming gang scandal shocked Britain, the perpetrators have been jailed, reforms have been introduced and institutions have apologised. Yet for many survivors and residents, questions about accountability, trust and whether justice has truly been delivered remain unanswered.
articles.content_html:
More than a decade has passed since the Rochdale child sexual exploitation scandal exposed one of the gravest safeguarding failures in modern British history. The men responsible have been convicted and imprisoned, but the question that continues to confront Rochdale is whether justice ended with those convictions.

Successive independent inquiries have reached strikingly similar conclusions. Reviews by Parliament, local safeguarding bodies and independent investigators found that vulnerable children were repeatedly failed by institutions responsible for protecting them. Victims were too often viewed as making 'lifestyle choices' rather than recognised as children subjected to coercion, rape, trafficking and organised sexual exploitation. Information was not consistently shared between agencies, warning signs were missed, organised offending was underestimated and opportunities to intervene were repeatedly lost.

The testimony of survivors remains among the most compelling evidence of those failures. Girls described repeatedly reporting abuse only to be disbelieved, dismissed as troublesome teenagers or treated as willing participants in their own exploitation. Children who regularly went missing were returned to the same environments where offenders continued to target them. Independent reviews concluded that professionals frequently focused on victims' behaviour rather than the methods of coercion used by organised offenders.

The criminal justice system eventually delivered significant convictions. Operation Span resulted in nine men being convicted in 2012 for offences including rape, trafficking and conspiracy to engage in sexual activity with children. Further investigations have led to additional prosecutions linked to historic child sexual exploitation across Greater Manchester. Judges described the offending as calculated, organised and profoundly damaging, recognising that many victims would carry lifelong psychological trauma.

Yet convictions answered only one question: the guilt of the offenders. They did not answer why children were repeatedly failed before those prosecutions ever reached a courtroom.

The official inquiries found that the primary problem was not an absence of legislation. The criminal offences already existed. Rather, agencies failed to recognise organised grooming, safeguarding procedures were inconsistently applied, intelligence was not always effectively shared and vulnerable children were too often judged instead of protected. Some reviews also concluded that concerns about community tensions influenced professional decision-making in certain cases, although they stressed that institutional failures were complex and involved multiple contributing factors.

Political debate over those failures continues today. Sir Keir Starmer has consistently defended his record as Director of Public Prosecutions, pointing to reforms introduced after the Rochdale prosecutions that encouraged prosecutors to focus more closely on suspect behaviour rather than relying heavily on assessments of victim credibility. Nigel Farage has repeatedly argued that institutional accountability remains incomplete and has called for wider national inquiries into organised child sexual exploitation.

Independent MP Rupert Lowe commissioned his own inquiry into grooming gangs, arguing that previous investigations had failed to provide full transparency or accountability. Lowe's report calls for mandatory recording of offender ethnicity, stronger criminal justice responses, improved national data collection and further investigation into institutional failings. While his inquiry does not carry statutory authority, it has become part of the continuing national debate surrounding organised child sexual exploitation and institutional responsibility.

London Mayor Sadiq Khan also faced criticism after asking for clarification during a London Assembly meeting about what was meant by the phrase 'grooming gangs' before responding more broadly on child sexual exploitation. The exchange became part of the wider political discussion over how public authorities describe organised abuse and communicate with victims and the public.

There have unquestionably been improvements since the original scandal. Greater Manchester Police has established dedicated child sexual exploitation capabilities, multi-agency safeguarding arrangements have been strengthened, inspection reports have recognised improvements in identifying vulnerable children and historic offenders continue to face prosecution years after their crimes. Those reforms are significant and should not be dismissed.

However, reform is not the same as accountability.

For many survivors, organisational apologies and revised procedures have never fully addressed the institutional failures identified by successive inquiries. Former Greater Manchester Police detective Maggie Oliver has repeatedly argued that child sexual exploitation remains a continuing threat and has warned against believing the lessons of Rochdale have been fully learned. She has consistently maintained that safeguarding depends not only on procedures but on professionals who are prepared to challenge assumptions, recognise organised exploitation and place children's welfare above institutional reputation.

Child sexual exploitation has not disappeared. Police forces across England and Wales continue to investigate organised grooming offences while offenders increasingly exploit social media, encrypted messaging platforms, online coercion and county lines criminality. Organised abuse evolves. Safeguarding must evolve with it.

The greatest lesson from Rochdale is not that Britain lacked the legal powers to prosecute offenders. It is that institutions repeatedly failed to use those powers when vulnerable children first asked for help. Children who should have been believed were doubted. Warning signs that should have triggered intervention were overlooked. Opportunities to prevent further abuse were lost.

Rochdale Borough Council has acknowledged profound institutional failings and apologised to survivors. Public bodies have accepted that serious mistakes were made, while successive reforms have sought to strengthen safeguarding and improve inter-agency cooperation. Those changes deserve recognition.

Whether they have fully restored public trust is another question entirely.

Justice cannot be measured solely by the length of prison sentences imposed on offenders. It is also measured by whether institutions learn from catastrophic failure, whether public officials accept responsibility when safeguarding collapses and whether every vulnerable child reporting abuse today can expect to be believed, protected and acted upon without hesitation.

Until survivors believe those standards have been achieved, and until the public is confident that institutional accountability carries meaningful consequences as well as organisational reform, many will continue to conclude that justice in Rochdale remains unfinished.

articles.title: Kirkholt and the fight against knife crime: why prevention matters as much as policing
articles.excerpt: Knife crime remains a concern for many families in Kirkholt, but police, youth workers and community groups say prevention, education and opportunity are just as important as enforcement in keeping young people safe.
articles.content_html:
Knife crime remains one of the issues that concerns many families across Kirkholt and the wider Rochdale borough. While high-profile incidents often make headlines, community leaders, police and youth organisations all agree that preventing young people from carrying knives in the first place is just as important as enforcing the law against those who do.

Although Rochdale has lower levels of knife crime than several other parts of Greater Manchester, it continues to experience incidents involving bladed weapons, particularly in areas facing higher levels of deprivation. The borough's Strategic Threat Assessment notes that knife crime is more common in town centres and some residential neighbourhoods where poverty is greatest, while young people are disproportionately affected as both victims and offenders. It also found that some children told youth workers they carried knives because they believed it offered protection or improved their image among peers.

For communities such as Kirkholt, the challenge is not simply about policing but understanding why some young people feel the need to carry a weapon. Youth workers and charities frequently point to a combination of social pressures, fear of becoming a victim, exploitation by organised criminals, school exclusion, adverse childhood experiences and limited opportunities as factors that can increase vulnerability.

Greater Manchester Police has continued to target violent crime through proactive neighbourhood policing, stop-and-search powers where legally justified and intelligence-led operations against drug dealing and organised crime. Officers covering Balderstone and Kirkholt currently identify drug dealing, off-road bikes and wider neighbourhood crime as local priorities, with regular patrols aimed at disrupting criminal activity and reassuring residents.

There have also been encouraging signs across the borough. Greater Manchester Police says knife crime in Rochdale reduced during the second half of 2024 compared with the first six months of the year, while more than 100 knives were surrendered through permanent amnesty bins installed at local police stations. Officers say removing weapons from circulation is one part of a broader strategy to reduce serious violence.

Community organisations argue, however, that enforcement alone cannot solve the problem. Providing safe places for young people to spend time, investing in youth services, sports clubs and mentoring programmes, and creating better employment opportunities are all seen as essential to reducing the long-term appeal of gangs and weapon carrying.

Parents also have an important role. Talking openly about peer pressure, recognising changes in behaviour and encouraging children to seek help if they feel threatened can all help prevent situations from escalating. Schools across Greater Manchester continue to work alongside police and youth services to educate pupils about the devastating consequences of carrying knives, not only for victims but for those who choose to carry them.

For most people living in Kirkholt, knife crime is not something they encounter in everyday life. The vast majority of residents simply want safe streets, strong communities and opportunities for young people to succeed. Nevertheless, every incident involving a knife has the potential to leave lasting consequences for families and neighbourhoods.

Reducing knife crime ultimately depends on a combination of effective policing, early intervention and community support. While officers continue to target those involved in serious violence, many local organisations believe the greatest success will come from ensuring fewer young people ever feel the need to pick up a knife in the first place.

articles.title: Rochdale-born TikToker investigated by Scottish police over Meta smart glasses videos
articles.excerpt: A Rochdale-born TikTok creator known online as 'E Dobbin' is being investigated by Scottish police after complaints relating to videos recorded using Meta smart glasses.
articles.content_html:
Scott Margerison, a Rochdale native who publishes content online under the alias 'E Dobbin', is being investigated by Scottish police following complaints about videos allegedly recorded using Meta smart glasses during a trip around Scotland.

According to the Daily Record, officers are reviewing footage to determine whether any criminal offences have been committed. The reported videos include members of the public, retail staff and CalMac employees being recorded, along with confrontational interactions and footage from the bridge of the CalMac ferry Loch Seaforth. CalMac subsequently suspended public bridge visits.

Previous controversies

The Scotland investigation is not the first controversy surrounding Margerison's online activity. He previously attracted significant public criticism after uploading footage filmed inside JD Gym in which viewers alleged he made racist and sexually explicit remarks while recording members of the public. Reports at the time indicated he was subsequently banned from the gym.

Online content

Across multiple TikTok accounts, some of which are no longer available, Margerison has published videos promoting numerous conspiracy theories and alternative historical claims. These include the Tartaria conspiracy theory, claims that the Apollo Moon landings were faked, the so-called Kalergi Plan conspiracy theory, and claims that mountains are the fossilised remains of enormous petrified creatures.

The Kalergi Plan conspiracy theory has been widely rejected by historians and researchers and is commonly associated with antisemitic conspiracy narratives.

Many of Margerison's videos challenge established historical, archaeological and scientific consensus and have generated substantial debate and criticism online.

Police investigation

Scottish police have confirmed officers received complaints and are reviewing the available material to establish whether any criminal offences have been committed.

At the time of publication no criminal charges have been announced. An investigation does not imply criminal guilt.
